Why we moved our nightly jobs off cron

Forty scheduled jobs, one overloaded box, and the boring queue that replaced them.

Hana Kowalczyk Oct 7, 2026 — 6 min read

For six years, every nightly job at Loomfield ran from a single crontab on a machine we called batch-01. Billing exports, search reindexing, and the customer usage reports all started at 2 a.m., and for a long time that was fine.

By this spring the crontab had grown to forty entries, and the jobs had started to overlap. When reindexing ran long, billing exports would start on a box with no free memory, fail halfway through, and leave partial files for the finance team to clean up by hand.

What we tried first

Our first fix was to spread the start times out, which helped for about a month. Then a large customer doubled their data, reindexing took twice as long, and we were back where we started. Staggering start times only works if you know how long every job takes, and we didn’t.

The queue

We replaced cron with a small job queue on top of our existing Postgres database. A scheduler inserts one row per job each night, and a pool of workers claims rows with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so no job runs twice and no worker sits idle while others are busy.

INSERT INTO jobs (name, run_after)
SELECT name, date_trunc('day', now()) + start_offset
FROM schedules
ON CONFLICT (name, run_after) DO NOTHING;

Failed jobs are retried with a delay, and after three failures they are parked and a message is posted to the on-call channel. The whole system is about four hundred lines of Go, and we have not had a partial billing export since June.

If you want to read more about the pattern, the Postgres documentation on row locking is a good place to start.
